question: What is the primary goal of the Drug Revolving Fund in public hospitals?

options.A: To provide a steady and uninterrupted supply of essential drugs
options.B: To supply free medications to every citizen
options.C: To pay salaries for the hospital pharmacy staff
options.D: To generate heavy profits for hospital management

explanation: The primary design of the DRF scheme is to prevent stockouts and maintain continuous drug availability through a self-sustaining financial loop. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why was the DRF introduced to replace traditional government drug budgets?

options.A: Traditional budgets were managed exclusively by international donors
options.B: Traditional budgets suffered from bureaucratic delays and frequent stockouts
options.C: Pharmacists refused to work with centralized government budgets
options.D: Government budgets made medicines too expensive for the poor

explanation: Bureaucratic delays in government funding releases often held up drug purchases. The DRF avoids this by keeping money inside the facility to buy stock quickly. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h1)

question: What is the name of the initial money used to start a DRF scheme?
explanation: Seed capital represents the initial financial investment required to purchase the first stock of medicines before the revolving cycle takes over. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h2)

question: A clinic receives seed capital from the state government. What must happen to this money for the DRF to work?

options.A: It must be shared as allowances among the hospital pharmacists
options.B: It must be used to purchase the first batch of essential medicines
options.C: It must be returned to the government treasury at the end of the month
options.D: It must be deposited into a fixed-deposit account to earn high interest

explanation: Seed capital is converted into drugs, which are sold to patients to generate the cash needed to keep the cycle moving. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h2)

question: Where does an established hospital DRF get most of its daily revenue?

options.A: Bank loans acquired by the pharmacy department
options.C: End-of-year donations from private pharmaceutical companies

explanation: Patient payments for medications at the hospital pharmacy provide the continuous cash flow needed to restock depleted medicines. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h3)

question: Why is a small markup added to the cost of drugs in a DRF?

options.A: To generate massive profits for hospital expansion projects
options.B: To pay bonuses to the medical director and chief pharmacist
options.C: To discourage patients from buying too many medications
options.D: To cover operational losses, expiration, and inflation

explanation: A small markup protects the fund against losses from damaged stock, expired items, and rising market prices so the capital value does not shrink. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which organization type acts as a third-party payer for enrolled patients in a DRF?
explanation: Health insurance agencies reimburse healthcare facilities for medicines provided to registered members, injecting formal funds into the DRF. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h4)

question: A hospital relies heavily on health insurance for its DRF. What common challenge happens with this funding?

options.A: Patients refuse to collect their prescribed drugs from the pharmacy
options.B: Insurance schemes prevent the pharmacy from stocking essential antibiotics
options.C: Delays in processing and paying claims can create temporary cash flow gaps
options.D: Managed care organizations dictate the exact staff salaries in the hospital

explanation: Late payments from insurance administrators can tie up funds and slow down the immediate purchase of fast-moving drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h4)

question: What form do external donations to a hospital DRF usually take?

options.A: Mandatory tax deductions from local businesses
options.B: Unrestricted personal loans for the medical staff
options.C: Foreign currency stored in private bank accounts
options.D: Targeted commodity grants and free drug supplies

explanation: Donors frequently supply specific disease-control medicines or medical consumables to support public health interventions in healthcare facilities. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h5)

question: Why must pharmacy managers handle free donor medications carefully in a DRF setup?

options.A: Donated drugs are usually expired before they reach the hospital
options.B: Patients reject donated medicines because they are considered low quality
options.C: Donors require the hospital to pay back the cost after one year
options.D: Mixing them improperly with revolving stock can distort pricing and inventory data

explanation: Clear separation of donated commodities prevents confusion between free stock and items purchased through revolving capital. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h5)

question: What are retained earnings in a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Unsold expired medications returned to the wholesale manufacturer
options.B: Surplus funds generated from drug sales that are reinvested into the fund
options.C: Profits withdrawn by the hospital management for personal use
options.D: Taxes collected by the government from private pharmacy shops

explanation: Retained earnings are financial surpluses kept within the DRF account to strengthen capital and expand drug availability. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h6)

question: What happens if DRF earnings are used to pay non-pharmacy hospital bills?

options.A: The hospital will automatically qualify for larger government grants
options.B: The pharmacy will be able to buy more expensive specialist drugs
options.C: The drug revolving fund will gradually collapse due to capital depletion
options.D: Patient attendance at the outpatient department will increase rapidly

explanation: Diverting capital out of the revolving loop leaves insufficient cash to replace sold medications, leading directly to stockouts. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which practice directly threatens the survival of a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Adjusting drug prices to match wholesale inflation rates
options.B: Keeping clear financial records of all daily transactions
options.C: Conducting regular physical stock counts of all medicines
options.D: Extending unauthorized credit sales to staff and patients

explanation: Unrecovered credit sales drain the cash pool, making it impossible to purchase replacement drugs from suppliers. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h7)

question: A clinic pharmacy has low cash to buy basic drugs despite high patient turnout. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Patients are refusing to get sick during the rainy season
options.B: Unaccounted stock losses, pilferage, or uncollected credit sales are draining the fund
options.C: The clinic is receiving too many free donations from NGOs
options.D: The government has increased the seed capital of the facility too much

explanation: A mismatch between high patient turnover and low cash reserves points directly to revenue leakage through theft, credit, or poor accounting. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h7)
